title: How the Internet Works
subtitle: The internet is just computers passing notes
objectives: Explain what actually happens when you open a website
Describe how packets, IP addresses, and DNS get data to the right place
Trace a request from your browser to a server and back
Tell the difference between TCP and UDP and when each is used

exercises.prompt: You open a website. Roughly how many separate computers might your request pass through before it reaches the server?
exercises.why: Your data hops through many routers along the way — often 10 to 20 — each one passing it a step closer to the destination. You can watch this happen yourself: run `traceroute google.com` (or `tracert` on Windows) and it prints every hop your packets take across the world.

exercises.prompt: Data doesn't travel as one big blob. It's broken into small chunks called ______.
exercises.why: The internet splits your data into small packets, sends them independently, and reassembles them at the other end. Because they travel independently, packets can take *different routes* and arrive out of order — so something has to put them back in sequence, which is TCP's job in lesson 4.

exercises.prompt: Every device on the internet needs one of these to be found. What is it?
exercises.why: An IP address (like `142.250.72.14`) is a device's location on the internet — data can't be delivered without one. There aren't enough of the old IPv4 addresses (~4.3 billion) for the world, which is exactly why IPv6 exists with an address space large enough that running out stops being a concern.

exercises.prompt: Match each piece to what it does.

pairs.right: A small chunk of your data
A device's location on the internet

exercises.why: Packets carry the data, IP addresses say where it's going, and routers move it hop by hop. The surprising part is that no router knows the whole path — each one only knows the *next best hop*, so the internet has no central map of itself.

exercises.prompt: There's no master computer running the internet. So how do packets find their way?
choices: A central server in the US decides every route
Each router just forwards to the next-best hop toward the target
Packets are sent to every computer until one matches
Your ISP pre-computes the full path
exercises.why: The internet is decentralized: each router makes a local decision — *who gets me closer?* — and no single machine is in charge. That's precisely why it's so resilient. Knock out a router and traffic simply routes around it, which was a design goal from its Cold-War-era origins rather than a happy accident.

exercises.prompt: You type `google.com`, but computers route by IP address. Who turns the name into the number?
exercises.why: DNS (Domain Name System) is the internet's phonebook — it looks up `google.com` and returns its IP address. Humans remember names and machines need numbers, so DNS is the translation layer that lets us live in a world of words.

exercises.prompt: DNS translates a human-friendly ______ into a machine-friendly IP address.
exercises.why: A domain name like `netflix.com` is for humans; DNS converts it to the IP address machines actually use to route packets.

exercises.prompt: Put a DNS lookup in order (simplified).
steps: Browser asks: what's the IP for `example.com`?
Check the local cache — seen it recently?
If not cached, ask a DNS resolver
exercises.why: DNS checks the fastest source first (the local cache) before asking a resolver, then hands the browser an IP to connect to. Results get cached at many levels — browser, operating system, resolver — each honouring a TTL (time to live), which is why a DNS change can take hours to reach everyone.

exercises.prompt: In October 2016, a company called Dyn was attacked. Suddenly Twitter, Spotify, Reddit, and Netflix all went dark at once — even though those companies were fine. What had been knocked out?
exercises.why: Dyn was a big DNS provider, and taking out DNS means users can't translate names to IPs — so the sites become unreachable while running perfectly. DNS is a quiet single point of failure for huge chunks of the web, which is why serious systems use multiple DNS providers.

exercises.prompt: Why does DNS cache results instead of looking up every time? Select all that apply.
choices: Lookups take time — caching makes pages load faster
It reduces load on DNS servers
It makes the answer more accurate
The same names are requested over and over
exercises.why: Caching is about speed and load: popular names are requested constantly, so remembering the answer avoids a repeat round trip. It does NOT make answers more accurate — a stale cache can happily serve an outdated IP. This is your first taste of caching, a theme you'll meet everywhere: keep the hot answer close, and accept that it might be behind.

exercises.prompt: Before your browser can send an HTTP request to a server, what does it need first?
exercises.why: You can't send data anywhere without a destination address, so DNS supplies the server's IP first — and only then can the request travel.

exercises.prompt: Order what happens when you visit `example.com`.
steps: DNS resolves `example.com` to an IP address
Browser opens a connection to that IP
Server sends back an HTTP response
exercises.why: Every page load is this dance: name → IP → connect → ask → process → answer → render. On a real HTTPS site there's also a TLS handshake right after connecting, which encrypts everything — that's the *s* in `https`.

exercises.prompt: Place the missing piece: your browser needs to turn `example.com` into an IP before reaching the server.
exercises.why: DNS sits between you and the server on that first step, translating the name so your browser knows where to connect.

exercises.prompt: Light travels fast, but not instantly. A round trip from New York to a server in London and back is roughly how many milliseconds — at the physical minimum?
exercises.why: Even at the speed of light through fibre, a New York–London round trip takes roughly 70ms. Physics sets a floor on latency that no amount of engineering can beat — which is why companies put servers *close to users* rather than trying to make the trip faster. You can't outrun light, so you shorten the distance.

exercises.prompt: Your page felt slow. The server responded in 5ms, but the total was 300ms. Where did the time most likely go?
exercises.why: If the server itself only took 5ms, the other 295ms was the network — the round trips of getting data there and back. A useful rule of thumb: the *network*, not the server, is often your latency bottleneck, so measure before you optimize.

lessons.title: TCP vs UDP: reliable vs fast

exercises.prompt: You're loading a bank statement. Every byte must arrive, in order, no errors. Which protocol fits?
exercises.why: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) guarantees delivery and order — it re-sends lost packets and reassembles them correctly, which is what you want for data you can't afford to lose. It manages that with acknowledgements: the receiver confirms each chunk, and anything unconfirmed gets re-sent, so reliability costs you extra round trips.

exercises.prompt: You're on a live video call. A dropped frame is fine, but a 2-second delay to re-send it is not. Which protocol fits?
exercises.why: UDP (User Datagram Protocol) just fires packets and doesn't wait for confirmation. For live audio and video, a missing frame beats a laggy one — speed matters more than perfection. This is a classic tradeoff you'll make again and again: reliability against latency.

exercises.prompt: Match the use case to the better protocol.
exercises.why: TCP for anything that must arrive complete and correct; UDP for small or real-time traffic where speed beats perfection. DNS traditionally uses UDP because a lookup is tiny — if it's lost, just ask again — while modern DNS-over-HTTPS uses TCP for privacy.

exercises.prompt: You're designing a multiplayer game's networking. Slide toward what you'd prioritize for player-movement updates.
exercises.why: For fast-moving player positions, low latency wins: a slightly stale position that arrives NOW beats a perfect one that arrives late. Games send fresh position updates constantly, so a lost one is instantly replaced — meaning TCP's re-sending of old positions would actually make gameplay feel *worse*.

exercises.prompt: The core tradeoff between TCP and UDP: TCP gives you reliability, UDP gives you ______.
exercises.why: TCP trades speed for guaranteed, ordered delivery; UDP trades those guarantees for raw speed. Neither is 'better' — the right choice depends entirely on what your system values most, and making that judgment *is* system design.

exercises.prompt: You've now traced a request end to end. Which statement best captures how the internet moves your data?
choices: One connection sends the whole file at once with no addressing
Data is split into packets, addressed by IP, routed hop-by-hop, and reassembled
A central server copies data directly to your screen
The browser stores everything locally and never contacts a server
exercises.why: That's the whole picture: split into packets, addressed with IPs (found via DNS), routed hop-by-hop by routers, and reassembled — reliably with TCP or fast with UDP. Everything else in this course — caching, load balancing, databases — is built on this foundation.
